fields.h1: All of Grace by Charles Spurgeon: Summary and Study Guide
fields.meta_title: All of Grace by Spurgeon — Summary & Study Guide
fields.description: A reader's study guide to Charles Spurgeon's All of Grace: a chapter-by-chapter summary of his plainspoken gospel classic on free grace, faith, and assurance, with themes, who should read it, and reflection questions. Read the full text free on Ochorus.
fields.body_html:
If you have ever suspected that you are too far gone for God to save, All of Grace was written for you. Charles Spurgeon put it plainly in his opening line: he would be “greatly disappointed if it does not lead many to the Lord Jesus.” This short book is the Prince of Preachers turning from his thousands and speaking to one anxious reader, pressing a single message until it lands — that God saves sinners by grace, as a free gift, and that the way in is not self-improvement but simple trust in Christ. This study guide summarizes the book, traces its argument chapter by chapter, and offers ways to read it today. The full text is free to read on Ochorus, and the guide is meant to send you into it.

What the book is, and what Spurgeon set out to do

All of Grace is a gospel primer, written in 1886 near the close of a ministry spent preaching to crowds of five and six thousand in London. It is the shortest book on Spurgeon’s shelf and the one he most often gave away. He wrote it for a very particular reader: someone who is not yet a Christian and half-suspects they are beyond hope. The whole book is addressed as “you,” and it moves through objections in the order people actually raise them — I am not good enough, I cannot feel anything, I have tried before, I do not know how to believe.

Spurgeon’s aim is not to impress but to rescue. He deliberately chose, in his words, “the very plainest language,” full of homely illustrations a servant could follow and a scholar could not fault. His single burden is to bring the worried, striving reader to rest — to move them off the treadmill of earning God’s favor and onto the firm ground of grace already given. The text beneath the whole book is Ephesians 2:8, and the title is the argument: if any part of salvation depended on the reader’s goodness, the reader would be lost. Which is exactly why they are not.

Here is my fountain, and here is my cup: find fault if you please; but do drink of the water of life.

Charles Spurgeon

How the book unfolds

The twenty short chapters form a single, patient argument, and it helps to see the path Spurgeon walks. He begins (“To You,” “What Are We At?”) by taking the anxious reader by the hand and naming the trouble: we keep looking for something good in ourselves before we dare come to God.

He then plants his flag on a startling text, Romans 4:5 — the God who “justifieth the ungodly.” This is the book’s foundation. Spurgeon insists that God does not wait for us to become worthy; He forgives the guilty as guilty. In his own words, God “makes those just who are unjust, forgives those who deserve to be punished, and favors those who deserve no favor.” Because God sees through every pretence, He knows, as Scripture says, that “there is none righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10) and that “all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags” (Isaiah 64:6). So Christ did not come to reward goodness but to save sinners.

From there Spurgeon turns to grace as the source (“By Grace Through Faith”). Salvation flows from God’s character, not ours:

It is not because of anything in them, or that ever can be in them, that they are saved; but because of the boundless love, goodness, pity, compassion, mercy, and grace of God.

Charles Spurgeon

Next he answers the practical question every reader asks — what is this faith I keep hearing about? Spurgeon’s famous definition follows: faith is made up of knowledge, belief, and trust. Knowledge comes first, for “faith cometh by hearing” (Romans 10:17) and “how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard?” (Romans 10:14). He illustrates faith with the eye that looks and the hand that grasps, and he explains why God chose faith as the channel of salvation — because, like an open hand, it simply receives what grace gives.

Faith is the simplest of all things, and perhaps because of its simplicity it is the more difficult to explain.

Charles Spurgeon

The later chapters carry the new believer forward. Spurgeon deals with the change God works within (“Regeneration and the Holy Spirit”), echoing the Lord’s own words that “ye must be born again” (John 3:7) and Paul’s that we are saved “not by works of righteousness which we have done” (Titus 3:5). He treats repentance as God’s gift rather than our achievement, and he closes with assurance — why those God saves will finally persevere, and why the anxious need not live in the fear of falling away. The last chapter (“Close”) is a personal appeal: Spurgeon says he laid down his pen to pray for every reader by name.

The central themes

Grace, not works. This is the beating heart of the book. Every good instinct that says “make yourself better first” is precisely what Spurgeon works to dismantle. Ephesians 2:8 is his keynote, and its next verse, that salvation is “not of works, lest any man should boast” (Ephesians 2:9), is never far away.

God justifies the ungodly. Spurgeon labors over Romans 4:5 and the paradox it holds together — that a holy God can declare a guilty sinner righteous without ceasing to be just. The cross is the answer: God is “just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus” (Romans 3:26), for Christ was made sin for us that we might be made righteous (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Faith as the empty hand. Spurgeon is at pains to show that faith is not itself a good work we perform to earn favor. It is the receiver, the open hand, the look of the eye toward the Saviour. To the reader who protests that they cannot believe well enough, he answers that they have misunderstood what is being asked.

Faith is the work of God’s grace in us.

Charles Spurgeon

Assurance and perseverance. Because salvation rests on grace and not on the believer’s performance, the same grace that begins the work will finish it. Spurgeon meets the “fear of final falling” head on and points the trembling reader back to the promise, not the pulse.

Who should read it

This is the book to hand to the seeker who feels unworthy — the person who wants to come to God but is convinced they must clean themselves up first. Spurgeon wrote it for exactly that person, and it has done that work for more than a century.

It is also for the anxious Christian who has never quite felt saved, who lives by feelings rather than by the promise, and who needs to hear that assurance rests on Christ and not on the strength of their own faith. Because it is short and utterly plain, it is a gift for new believers, for those exploring Christianity for the first time, and for anyone who finds heavier theology hard going. And it repays the mature reader too: pastors and long-time believers often return to it to recover the sheer freeness of the gospel they may have started to take for granted. If you want a companion volume, Spurgeon’s Around the Wicket Gate presses the same invitation on those lingering at the door, and D. L. Moody’s The Way to God covers the same ground with a revivalist’s warmth.

How to read it today

Read it slowly and personally. Spurgeon warns in his closing chapter that “book-reading is of small value unless the truths which pass before the mind are grasped, appropriated, and carried out.” This is not a book to skim for information; it is a book to be argued with and won over by. Where Spurgeon addresses “you,” let him mean you.

A few practical suggestions. Keep a Bible open beside it and look up the texts he leans on — Romans 4:5, Ephesians 2:8, and Isaiah 45:22, the “Look unto me, and be ye saved” that turned Spurgeon’s own life around at fifteen. Read one or two short chapters a day rather than racing through; the argument is cumulative and rewards patience. Notice the objections he answers and mark the one that is yours — most readers find their own excuse somewhere in these pages. And do not stop at understanding. Spurgeon’s whole point is that the gospel is to be received, the way an open hand receives a gift; his final plea is that you would actually “lay hold upon Christ Jesus.”

It is all in vain, dear reader, that you and I have met, unless you have actually laid hold upon Christ Jesus, my Lord.

Charles Spurgeon

The nineteenth-century idiom is gentle and easily followed, but if a phrase snags, the illustrations almost always unlock it — Spurgeon rarely leaves a hard point without a homely picture beside it. You can read the whole thing in an afternoon, and many have, but its truths are worth carrying for a lifetime.

For reflection and discussion

Whether you read alone or with a group, these questions can help the book do its work.

  • Spurgeon says God “justifieth the ungodly” (Romans 4:5). Do you find yourself waiting to become worthy before you come to God? What would change if you took him at his word that grace is for the ungodly now?
  • Spurgeon defines faith as knowledge, belief, and trust, and calls it the hand that receives rather than a work that earns. How does that reframe the worry, “I cannot believe well enough”?
  • Ephesians 2:8 is the book’s keynote — “by grace are ye saved, through faith.” Where are you still quietly trying to add your own works to grace, and what would it look like to stop?
  • Spurgeon meets the “fear of final falling” by pointing to God’s keeping rather than our gripping. Does your sense of security rest on Christ’s faithfulness or on the strength of your own feelings?
  • In his closing chapter Spurgeon says the book is in vain unless the reader has “laid hold upon Christ.” Reading it now, what is your response — and what is the next step you will take?

You can read All of Grace in full, free of charge, on Ochorus, and explore more of the life and writing of Charles H. Spurgeon. If it stirs you, carry it further with D. L. Moody and the other plainspoken gospel classics on the shelf — but first, do as Spurgeon asked, and drink of the water of life.
